entry.title: Spacepower 2024 — notes from Orlando
entry.content:
I went to Spacepower 2024 in Orlando as one of five winners of the UF Space Initiative 2024 Innovation Challenge. The Space Force Association previewed our team in its official magazine, calling us “a dynamic group who embodied the power of cross-disciplinary collaboration.” That line — and the bright orange WINNER badge on my lanyard — made this one a real personal milestone.

Why it mattered

  • First serious dive into the space sector. It was the first room where my anthropology habit and my AI toolkit were obviously on the same side.
  • Startup-first atmosphere. Panels on venture funding, SpaceWERX accelerators, and small-sat constellations showed how fast ideas move from lab to launchpad.
  • Hands-on demos. Tried an AI-enabled space-debris tracker, tested a digital-twin trainer for Guardians, and saw live inference on orbit-qualified edge GPUs.

Conference highlights

  • Maj Gen Timothy Sejba (Commander, STARCOM) — keynote on building a “purpose-built” Space Force ready for Great-Power competition.
  • Startup showcase — 30+ early-stage companies pitching propulsion, on-orbit servicing, and AI autonomy. Many funded through the SpaceWERX Tactical Funding Increase program.
  • Gen-AI Challenge Finals — teams used Guardian fitness telemetry to generate personalized training plans. This is exactly the kind of multimodal pipeline work I enjoy — pulling signal from sensors you’d normally ignore.
  • One quote stuck with me: “Innovation is our orbital maneuver; agility is our delta-V.” — SFA President William Woolf.

Take-aways

  • Identified potential mentors in model-based systems engineering (MBSE) and satellite-AI inference for follow-up.
  • Sketched a capstone idea: an AI-powered, culture-aware knowledge base for long-duration missions — merging anthropology and CS.
  • Brought home concrete design cues for my own projects (edge ML for in-remote-sensing decision-making).

Read the SFA Pre-Spacepower Magazine (PDF) →
entry.summary: Attending Spacepower as a UF Space Initiative Innovation Challenge winner — keynotes, startups, and what I took back to the lab.

entry.title: SHPE National Convention 2024 — notes
entry.content:
Four days at the SHPE National Convention 2024. The database side of the convention was my own project; this post is just the attendee’s notebook.

Workshops that stuck

  • Amazon Career Readiness Talk — concrete framing on how to walk into technical interviews with a story, not just a résumé.
  • Professional Networking Event — standard playbook, but a good forcing function for practicing the 30-second version of my current work.
  • L3Harris Goal Setting 101 — simple structure, held up under pressure.
  • Northrop Grumman LGBT Leadership Panel — honest conversations about defense culture that you don’t get from the recruiting page.
  • John Deere and Automation — the AgTech crossover with my remote-sensing work was bigger than I’d expected.

Who I met

Representatives from Google, Apple, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and a long list of smaller firms. The Northrop line turned into the Mission Systems internship the following summer, which is probably the single highest-leverage connection I’ve made at any convention.

What I took back

  • A better pitch — specifically, how to compress the dual-major into one sentence that doesn’t read as “two unrelated hobbies.”
  • Realistic framing on managing multiple responsibilities and avoiding the overcommit trap that eats most student-leaders by senior year.
  • A clearer sense of how defense interviews differ from standard SWE interviews — different questions, different trust-building, different pacing.
  • The read that passion + expertise + character is the only package deal that cuts through at a 15k-person event.
entry.summary: Four days, 15,000 attendees, and the workshops that stuck — Amazon career readiness, L3Harris goal-setting, Northrop Grumman LGBT leadership, John Deere automation.

entry.title: Innovation Summit 2024 — notes
entry.content:
Spent a day at Innovation Summit 2024. Three speakers mattered, and one VC panel put the money side into context.

Speakers

  • Brian Mawdsley (Deputy CIO @ UFICO) — on finding meaning in work and investment analysis. Pushed hard on identifying the next thing rather than reasoning retroactively about what won. Quote: “Focus on the compass, not the clock.”
  • Jackson Streeter (Director @ UF Ventures) — the entrepreneur counterweight to Brian’s investor lens. Big on clean energy, business ecosystems, and the point that you should obsess over individual customers before you obsess over market trends.
  • Jack Kendall (CTO of Rain AI) — on neuromorphic computing and the future of AI compute. Shared the arc of developing patent-worthy work and underlined how often breakthroughs sit on multidisciplinary ground. The most directly relevant speaker to my BCI direction.

VC panel

  • Ryan Pruitt (Managing Director @ Ocean Azul Partners)
  • Olivia Gaudree (Managing Director @ Fuel VC)
  • Chris Langford (Managing Partner @ Home Tech Ventures)

The panel surfaced what VCs actually look for in founders — not just the pitch, but passion, expertise, and character as a package deal.

What I’m taking back

The Rain AI conversation was the one I keep coming back to. Neuromorphic hardware and real-time BCI/EEG are converging on the same bottleneck from opposite ends — one builds a chip that thinks like a brain, the other reads from an actual brain. There’s a company-shaped hole between them.
entry.summary: Three speakers, one VC panel, and the connection between neuromorphic computing and the BCI thesis I've been circling.
